title: introduce-mini-cache-hypervisor-with-batch-hinting-and-telemetry-feedback
author: Maya Chen
description:
Motivation:
This PR adds a lightweight, per-model "mini-cache hypervisor" and a runtime batch-hinting layer that uses live telemetry to adapt microcache lifetimes and batching signals. Production workloads exhibited uneven unit economics: short repeating prefixes caused wasted compute when cache TTLs were either too aggressive (stale misses) or too conservative (low hit rate). Existing cache/prefill knobs are coarse and require offline profiling.

What this PR does (single-string overview with sections):
- Implements a mini-cache hypervisor: a thin orchestration layer that sits between the request router and the model runtime. It evaluates incoming request signatures (prefix fingerprint, request size, priority) and applies microcache TTLs (50ms–2s) and selective KV-cache warmup hints at request time. The hypervisor does not modify model state; it only decides whether the runtime should attempt a KV prefetch or serve off a short lived cached result.
- Adds batch-hinting metadata emitted by the router: requests can carry a low-cost hint (batchable / prefer-latency / prefer-cost). The runtime uses hints to balance grouping and tail latency; hints are advisory and respected subject to SLO constraints.
- Telemetry feedback loop: a new econometrics job consumes per-request outcomes (hit/miss, additional tokens, end-to-end latency, cost-attribution) and produces per-model microcache profiles. Those profiles are pushed to the hypervisor as JSON presets and are applied conservatively (canary rollout).
- Safety and fallbacks: when a hypervisor profile is missing or confidence is low, we fall back to existing default caching behavior. Any adverse signal (increased generation errors, latency P99 regression, or cost spike > 20%) triggers automatic rollback for the model.

Design details and tradeoffs:
- TTL granularity and scope: TTLs are intentionally short (sub-second range) to target repeating conversational prefixes and high-QPS patterns. This avoids long-lived cache correctness concerns while still capturing common micro-repetition patterns.
- Lightweight decisions: evaluation path is optimized for minimal CPU cost. Fingerprinting is done with xxhash64 and a compact signature of the first n tokens and route metadata.
- Prioritization: the hypervisor respects request priority and can disable batching for explicit low-latency flags.
- Privacy: signatures are canonicalized and hashed; no raw tokens are stored in persistent profiles.

Testing and validation:
- Unit tests for hypervisor decision logic (edge cases: empty prefix, very long prefix, and context-window wrap).
- Integration tests that simulate high-QPS synthetic workloads to show 12–28% per-token cost reduction on warm micro-pattern traces and <5ms median added decision latency.
- Staging canary runs on dedicated capacity with shadow traffic for three weeks.

Rollout plan:
1) Merge behind feature flag `mini_cache_hypervisor_v1` and enabled only for experiments namespace.
2) Push profiles from econometrics job as managed configs; start with conservative TTLs (100ms) and 5% sample traffic.
3) Monitor metrics: per-model token-cost, end-to-end P99 latency, generation error-rate, and cache-hit ratio.
4) If stable, increase sample to 25% then 100% with gradual TTL tightening.

Related tickets and context: ENG-2981 (telemetry pipeline for econometrics), ENG-3042 (runtime batch hints API), and ops note SUP-412 for customers on Dedicated who opt out.

Checklist (author):
- [x] Implementation and unit tests
- [x] Integration harness and perf benchmark scripts
- [x] Canary config and rollback jobbook entries
- [x] Docs: runtime flags and admin console knobs

Backwards compatibility: The hypervisor is opt-in via feature flag. No API contract changes are required for customer traffic.

Merging notes: Squash-merge with changelog entry; target follow-up PR to move canary profiles into the managed-config service for dynamic updates.
